name: Scratchy Editorial Poster
description: An editorial magazine cover drawn in scratchy pen and marker over rough blocks of colour — two inks on stark white paper, the subject cropped tight, and huge distressed poster capitals bleeding behind it as pure texture.
style_bible: An editorial magazine cover, drawn fast and printed rough. Medium: scratchy pen and marker work laid over blocks of colour brushed in with a loaded, half-dry brush — the blocks are put down first and the drawing goes over the top, so the two never line up exactly and the colour runs past the line in places and stops short of it in others. Hatching is quick, angular and repeated: parallel scratches for shadow, crossed scratches for the deepest value, scribbled loops for tone, and bare paper wherever the form is lit. Nothing is filled in tidily and nothing is finished at the edges — contours break off mid-stroke, a shoulder ends in three unconnected marks, and a block of colour stops with a dry ragged edge rather than an outline. Surface: stark white paper, left as the dominant value across the frame, carrying visible tooth, small flecks and one or two honest smudges. Palette: strictly limited to two inks on that white — one dominant colour and one accent, chosen with the flat, slightly off-register punch of screen printing (vermilion and slate, mustard and ink blue, pink and black, teal and burnt orange), plus the black of the pen. The two inks overlap in a few places and where they overlap they make a third, darker value; there is no other colour anywhere and no gradient of any kind. Subject: one subject only, cropped tight and centred — a head and shoulders, a pair of hands, a held object, or a simple form — cut hard by the frame edge on at least two sides so it feels bigger than the page. Lettering as texture: enormous distressed poster capitals sit behind the subject and bleed off every edge, cut off by the figure and by the frame so no complete word is ever visible; they are printed in the accent ink, eroded and broken as if pulled from a worn block, and they exist only to give the background rhythm and scale. Treat them as ornament, not language: the real title is set by the caption system afterwards, so nothing in the picture needs to spell anything. Around the subject, mock body-copy columns of unreadable grey ruled lines, a folio mark, a couple of rules, and handwritten margin notes and arrows in the black pen complete the cover furniture. Framing: sixteen by nine, centred and frontal, the subject filling most of the height, the composition held together by the white and the two inks rather than by depth — flat, no perspective, no rendered space. Mood: urgent, printed overnight, opinionated. Keep the contract content-independent: no fixed individual, brand, publication, headline, place or copied composition.
